text:
The premise is false. Evidence is mixed: Bloom et al.'s randomized trial at Trip.com (Nature, 2024) found hybrid work (3 days in-office) had no effect on productivity or promotions and cut attrition by about a third. An earlier Ctrip trial found fully remote call-center work was more productive. A memo claiming "everyone agrees" will be easy to rebut.

What the evidence supports is narrower. Three defensible bullets, from memory, so verify figures before circulating:

- **Fully remote work can reduce output in some roles.** Atkin, Schoar and Shinde found about 18% lower productivity among fully remote data-entry workers in India. Gibbs, Mengel and Siemroth found roughly 4% lower productivity at an Asian IT firm, with longer hours.
- **Remote work weakens collaboration and mentorship.** Yang et al. (Nature Human Behaviour, 2022), using Microsoft data, found remote work made collaboration networks more siloed. Emanuel, Harrington and Pallais found junior engineers received less feedback when working remotely.
- **Remote video meetings produce fewer creative ideas.** Brucks and Levav (Nature, 2022) found video calls generated fewer ideas than in-person ones.

The strongest case against using these: they apply to specific roles and to fully remote setups, while the best hybrid evidence shows no productivity loss. If your board is weighing a return-to-office mandate, the more defensible memo argues for targeted in-person time for mentorship and creative work, not that remote work kills productivity.
